items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And when I write, I’m writing — like Oliver Lake —not Oliver Lake but Oliver Nelson — Oliver, Duke Ellington and my head is like that.

ctx.x: society. Now you’re describing this intense relationship with local musicians and spreading it worldwide and when I think back to the swing era that jazz and swing had this social dancing aspect and entertainment value. Do you have a thought about jazz in America now? Where does it fit? Does it have a distinctive character in America now?

Yeah, a lot of different jazz styles now as you know. You know I’m 80 years old. My concept comes out of — the genesis of my concept came from the 50s from the bebop era. And when I write, I’m writing — like Oliver Lake —not Oliver Lake but Oliver Nelson — Oliver, Duke Ellington and my head is like that. My head is grounded in that sound although I write all kinds of ways. I’ve got skills to write all kinds of ways you know. But you know I even learned how to deal with hip hop, I mean techno you know. Because I…
Well said. I like the term, the audience could digest. Something that is acceptable to them and they can get something out of.

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: So I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands. Ray Charles.

ctx.x: This is the brass over here and the reeds over here. And then you learn how to score. You put all this stuff in the score, that’s a whole different thing. I went to the Conservatory before I moved to New York. I was like 18 years old and I went to the Conservatory and I learned keyboard harmony and solfeggio and all that you know. And I learned how to write European music you know. Stravinsky or let’s say Beethoven or Mozart. I learned how to put it together. So now as I said, well how can I learn Duke Ellington…

see? Jazz wasn’t even considered music in a lot of camps you know. It was like rap music today, you know it was like, oh wow, that’s a whole different world, you know, ether. So I say, “Well that’s my interest.” So I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands. Ray Charles. And they was writing. They was writing for different groups and whatnot. Because like if you go to New York, at that particular time, you could actually — if…
